content: 1. Provide detailed and age-appropriate information to adolescent clients, their parents, and guardians about voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC), including its risks and benefits, while addressing any concerns they may have. 2. Support parents in their critical roles in adolescent development, such as preparing both boys and girls for puberty and fostering equitable gender norms. Parents also play a key role in facilitating adolescents' access to community-based interventions, such as HPV vaccination for girls. 3. Enhance parents' knowledge and address any misconceptions they may have to enable them to provide meaningful guidance to their children on sensitive topics like puberty, sexuality, and reproduction. 4. Monitor adverse events (AEs) among adolescents undergoing VMMC to better understand and mitigate risks. 5. Implement data-driven quality improvement strategies and plans at all levels of service delivery. 6. Ensure that all adolescents, regardless of their financial status, age, marital status, education level, ethnicity, sexual orientation, or other characteristics, have access to appropriate services in a manner that promotes their meaningful engagement and participation. 7. Create an enabling environment for healthcare workers and adolescent clients to effectively obtain, provide, and verify informed consent and assent. This includes investing in human resources to maintain and enhance competence in handling informed consent, drawing on lessons from other services and research. 8. Train healthcare workers to deliver person-centered adolescent services tailored to each stage of physical development. This includes training on assessing adolescents' capacity to consent, engaging parents in the informed consent process, and addressing age-specific developmental and physical considerations. 9. Equip healthcare workers with the technical competence to provide effective health services while upholding adolescents' rights to information, privacy, confidentiality, non-discrimination, non-judgmental attitudes, and respect. 10. Provide healthcare workers with refresher training to stay updated on age-appropriate approaches to HIV health education, counseling, and general adolescent care. 11. Understand the stages of adolescent development and assess maturity to ensure a meaningful, age-appropriate, and comprehensible informed consent process for every client. 12. Identify effective strategies to engage communities and parents in the delivery of maleand age-friendly health services. 13. Evaluate service delivery approaches designed to maintain high levels of VMMC coverage and assess the feasibility, effectiveness, and cost of providing additional services to adolescents beyond the minimum VMMC package. 14. Explore approaches that integrate VMMC into a broader package of adolescent health services, contributing to sustainable development goals and universal health coverage. 15. Assess the uptake of other health services among boys aged 10–14 years, including those advised to defer circumcision until they are older. 16. Identify effective training methods to enhance adolescent health services. 17. WHO recommends the use of WHO-prequalified male circumcision devices as additional methods for HIV prevention in males aged 15 years and older. This recommendation is conditional and based on moderate-quality evidence. 18. The use of these devices for adolescents aged 10–14 years may be considered when additional data become available. This recommendation is conditional and based on low-quality evidence. 19. These recommendations apply in settings where healthcare workers are appropriately trained and competent in using the specific devices, and where surgical backup facilities and skills are available as needed. 20. Device-based methods of male circumcision may offer some advantages over surgical methods, such as shorter procedure times, reduced loss of work or school time, and more consistent cosmetic results. However, these benefits are not yet clearly established. 21. Healing times after in situ device-based procedures are typically one to two weeks longer than after surgical circumcision due to healing by secondary intention. 22. Device-based methods are generally considered acceptable by most men and adolescent boys and are simpler and easier for healthcare providers to use. 23. The costs of device-based methods are similar to those of surgical methods, and scaling up their use may yield efficiencies. 24. Implementation and scale-up of device-based methods require post-market surveillance to ensure safety and effectiveness. 25. WHO prequalification of male circumcision devices ensures that specific devices meet international standards for product performance, quality management, and clinical safety and efficacy. Prequalification does not imply WHO approval or endorsement but provides assurance of quality for procurement by relevant agencies and programs. 26. The WHO Technical Advisory Group (TAG) on Innovations in Male Circumcision has expanded and revised device categories based on mechanism of action, including in situ devices, clamp devices, elastic collar compression devices, ligature compression devices, and surgical assist devices. 27. In situ devices remain in contact with the body for at least 24 hours and include several subtypes, such as collar clamp devices and elastic collar compression devices. 28. Clamp devices achieve rapid compression of the foreskin to prevent bleeding and allow immediate or near-immediate removal of the foreskin. Local anesthesia is required for pain control. 29. Elastic collar compression devices slowly compress the foreskin to induce ischemia, devitalization, and necrosis. The foreskin may be removed after seven days or excised shortly after device placement. Local anesthesia requirements depend on the timing of foreskin removal. 30. Ligature compression devices use a ring and flexible ligature to compress the foreskin, achieving hemostasis and allowing foreskin removal at the time of or shortly after device application. Local anesthesia is required. 31. Surgical assist devices are used during surgical circumcision and are removed at the end of the procedure. They include clamp devices and complex mechanisms that perform foreskin excision, hemostasis, and wound closure. 32. Evidence informing updated recommendations was based on data from devices that met the full set of required studies, including collar clamp devices (e.g., Shang Ring™), elastic collar compression devices (e.g., PrePex™), and surgical assist devices (e.g., Unicirc™). 33. The strength of the recommendations was influenced by the quality of evidence on critical outcomes (efficacy, safety, and acceptability), anticipated benefits and harms, client and healthcare worker preferences, and resource implications. 34. Further evidence is needed to demonstrate the safety and advantages of device-based methods at scale in routine healthcare settings, as well as to address uncertainties about patient acceptability and program costs.
